title: Review: Atoms and nuclear radiation
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Physics (8463) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.4.2-c11, 4.4.2-c28, 4.4.2-c06, 4.4.2-c25. Clues: 4.4.2-c11 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c28 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c06 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c25 written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: 4.4.2-q13, 4.4.2-q14, 4.4.2-q15, 4.4.2-q09, 4.4.2-q19, 4.4.2-q10, 4.4.2-q16, 4.4.2-q12, 4.4.2-q20, 4.4.2-q05, 4.4.2-q22, 4.4.2-q04. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Gamma ray (γ)
items.clue: Electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.

items.label: Peer review
items.clue: The checking of published findings by other scientists.

items.label: Count-rate
items.clue: The number of decays recorded each second by a detector.

items.label: Radioactive contamination
items.clue: The unwanted presence of unstable atoms on or in other materials.

questions.stem: In a smoke alarm the radiation crosses a small gap in air and is absorbed when smoke enters the gap. Which source is best, and why?

options.text: Gamma, because it is the most penetrating and always reaches the sensor.
Gamma, because the most penetrating source is always the best choice.
Gamma, because alpha is too weak to cross even a small air gap.
Alpha, because it ionises strongly and is absorbed over a short range in air.

questions.explanation: Alpha's strong ionisation and few-centimetre range mean smoke in the gap changes the reading.

questions.stem: A paper mill measures the thickness of paper by detecting radiation that passes through it. Which source should be chosen?

options.text: Beta, because the amount getting through changes as the thickness changes.
Alpha, because it ionises most strongly and gives the largest reading of all.
Gamma, because it passes through the paper without being changed.
Alpha, because it is the safest radiation for the workers to be near.

questions.explanation: Paper partly absorbs beta, so the count-rate responds to small changes in thickness.

questions.stem: A tracer is injected into a patient and its progress is followed by a detector held outside the body. Which source is most suitable?

options.text: An alpha emitter, because alpha ionises most and is the easiest to detect.
A gamma emitter, because gamma passes out through the body tissue.
An alpha emitter, because paper stops alpha so it is harmless inside.
A beta emitter, because beta is stopped by skin and stays inside.

questions.explanation: Only gamma is penetrating enough to leave the body and reach an external detector.

questions.stem: A beta source is placed near a detector and different absorbers are tried. Which description of beta radiation is correct?

options.text: It is less penetrating than alpha because it is a lighter particle.
It ionises more strongly than an alpha particle and is stopped by card.
It is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium and travels about a metre in air.
It passes right through aluminium and is only reduced by thick lead.

questions.explanation: Beta's penetration and range in air, the two properties the specification requires.

questions.stem: A nucleus emits a beta particle. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?

options.text: The mass falls by 1 and the charge of the nucleus increases by 1.
The mass does not change and the charge of the nucleus falls by 1.
The mass does not change but the charge increases by 1.
Both the mass and the charge of the nucleus fall by 1.

questions.explanation: A neutron becomes a proton, so the nucleon count holds and the charge rises.

options.text: A heavy particle with no charge that is thrown out of the nucleus.
Radiation given out when an electron moves between two shells.
A tiny uncharged particle shot out from inside the nucleus.
Electromagnetic radiation given out from the nucleus of an atom.

questions.explanation: The specification's own description of a gamma ray.

questions.stem: In a nuclear equation, which symbol represents an alpha particle?

options.text: The symbol ²₄He, with the 2 written above the 4.
The symbol ⁰₋₁e, an electron from the nucleus.
The symbol ⁴₂He, which is a helium nucleus.
The symbol ¹₁H, which is a single proton leaving.

questions.explanation: The specification represents an alpha particle by ⁴₂He.

questions.stem: Some unstable nuclei emit a neutron. Which statement about this emission is correct?

options.text: A neutron cannot leave a nucleus, so this must really be beta decay.
A neutron (n) is one of the nuclear radiations a nucleus emits.
The neutron carries a negative charge out of the nucleus with it.
Neutron emission is another name for the release of a gamma ray.

questions.explanation: The specification lists a neutron (n) as one of the possible emissions.

questions.stem: When a nuclear equation for alpha decay is balanced, which quantities must be equal on both sides?

options.text: The number of protons only, as neutrons carry no charge.
The mass numbers only, as charge leaves with the alpha.
The number of neutrons on each side of the equation.
The total mass number and the total atomic number.

questions.explanation: Balancing is limited to making the mass numbers and the atomic numbers match.

questions.stem: Which list gives the types of nuclear radiation that an unstable nucleus may emit?

options.text: Alpha particles, beta particles, X-rays and neutrons.
Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and neutrons.
Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and protons.
Alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays only.

questions.explanation: These are the four emissions listed by the specification.

questions.stem: A nucleus emits a gamma ray. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?

options.text: The mass number falls a little because energy has been carried off.
The charge falls by one but the mass number is the same.
Neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus is changed at all.
The mass number falls by four and the charge falls by two.

questions.explanation: A gamma ray has no mass number and no charge, so both numbers are unchanged.

questions.stem: A student monitors a source with a Geiger-Muller tube. What is the count-rate?

options.text: The number of nuclei that decay in the whole source each second.
The energy given to the Geiger-Muller tube by radiation each second.
The number of decays the tube records, which is the activity.
The number of decays recorded each second by the detector.

questions.explanation: The specification's definition of count-rate exactly.
